title: Seed Backup Copies and Materials: Paper, Laminate, and Steel
plain:
Your recovery phrase is the only thing that rebuilds your wallet, so keeping a backup is essential. But every copy you make is also a copy that can be found. Weigh what an extra copy protects against what it exposes.

A second identical copy does protect against one danger: a single fire, flood, or lost slip no longer wipes you out. But it also doubles the number of places the words exist. If either copy is discovered, photographed, or stolen, the funds are gone. In plain terms, you have doubled the ways to lose the funds, not doubled the safety.

Decide deliberately how many copies you truly need. For most people, one or two carefully placed copies in separate, secure locations beat many scattered ones. Fewer copies means fewer leaks; more copies means better protection from destruction.

Materials matter as much as copy count. Paper is simple and cheap, but paper and laminate can still burn, melt or fade. House fires, floods, humidity, and even years of sunlight ruin paper more often than people expect, and lamination can trap moisture or melt near heat.

Metal is the durable upgrade: steel survives house fires and floods better than paper. A stamped or engraved steel plate can come through a fire that turns a paper copy to ash. It still must be hidden — steel resists fire and water, not discovery.

Whatever you choose: never photograph, scan, or type your recovery phrase into any computer, phone, or website. Store copies in separate secure locations, and confirm you can actually restore from a backup before depending on it.
technical:
Duplication is a trade-off between two failure modes: unavailability (the backup is destroyed or lost) and compromise (an unauthorized person reads it). Adding identical copies lowers the chance of total loss but raises cumulative discovery risk, because the security of the weakest copy governs the whole wallet. Sensible mitigations are geographic separation, tamper-evident storage, and — for advanced users only — a passphrase, remembering that a forgotten passphrase is itself a total-loss risk.

On materials: house fires commonly reach roughly 600–950 °C, above paper's ~230 °C ignition point and the softening range of common laminating plastics, while stainless steel melts near 1,400 °C and resists corrosion from flooding. Stamped or engraved characters outlast printed or handwritten marks under heat. No consumer medium survives every hazard, so match the medium to your realistic threats — fire, flood, corrosion, discovery — rather than assuming any single solution covers all.
